title: Why I Deleted My Browser Extension’s Onboarding Tour

A simpler layout What I’d tell other extension developers What’s next Chrome Extension Onboarding UX Design Indiehackers Product Management Why I Deleted My Browser Extension’s Onboarding Tour Ittikorn Longtee 4 min read · Nov 3, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Why I Deleted My Browser Extension’s Onboarding Tour Users were uninstalling on day one. What I learned about first impressions, and what I built instead. Press enter or click to view image in full size I’m an independent developer, and I build a free new tab extension called WanaGo. It shows a travel photo from more than 1,000 destinations every time you open a tab, with a bar underneath to search hotels and flights for that place. For a while I had a problem I couldn’t explain. People installed it, and then they were gone, often on the same day. This is the story of how I found the cause, why it was my own onboarding, and what I changed. The tour I was proud of The old version greeted new users with a five-step guided tour. A dark overlay covered the page, and tooltips pointed at each feature one by one: the search bar, the booking bar, the settings, the bucket list, the to-do list. It looked polished. It explained everything. And I now think it was the worst part of the product. First, find out who your users actually are When I opened the store analytics, my first surprise wasn’t about uninstalls. It was about installs. A large share of my installs came from one country, one operating system and had no language data at all. Real people don’t look like that. They looked like automated traffic, such as store crawlers or testing systems, rather than humans who chose to install the extension. Once I set those aside, the real picture was smaller but much clearer: among real users, most of the uninstalls happened on the same day as the install . Lesson 1: before you analyze behavior, make sure you’re looking at people. Bots inflate installs and hide the real retention rate. Why the tour was hurting A new tab extension has a very unusual first moment. The user opens a new tab because they want to do something: search, open a site, check an email. They didn’t open it to learn about my product. My tour got in their way at exactly that moment. It covered the page, asked for five clicks, and delayed the one thing they came for. From the user’s side, the first experience was: “I installed a pretty wallpaper and now something is blocking my browser.” I realized I had built onboarding for me , so I could show every feature I’d made, and not for the user, who only wanted to see a beautiful photo and keep working. Lesson 2: onboarding should never stand between the user and the reason they installed your product. What I built instead In version 3.0 I removed the forced tour and redesigned the first experience around a few simple ideas. 1. A welcome card that doesn’t block anything Now there’s a small card in the corner that says hello and explains WanaGo in one line. The page underneath works normally. The card appears only on the first few new tabs and then disappears for good, so it never becomes noise. Press enter or click to view image in full size 2. The tour still exists, but it’s optional Some people do like a guided tour. So there’s a “Take a quick tour” button on the welcome card, and a “Replay tour” option in Settings. Users choose it; it never chooses them. 3. Sensible defaults instead of questions The booking bar used to need setup before it was useful. Now it comes with reasonable defaults (dates and number of travelers already filled in), so the very first click works. People can change details later if they care. 4. Highlight one thing, not five Instead of pointing at every feature, the first tab gently highlights only the most important one, the booking bar, with a soft glow. Everything else is there to discover over time. 5. A simpler layout I also tried something clever: a single bar that flipped between “search Google” and “search hotels and flights”. It was compact, but people needed a hint to understand it. I replaced it with two plain bars stacked on top of each other. Less clever, much clearer. Lesson 3: if a design needs a tutorial to be understood, the design is the problem, not the lack of a tutorial. What I’d tell other extension developers Filter out bot installs before you trust any retention number. Measure same-day uninstalls. They tell you more about your first impression than any review. Deliver the core value in the first second. For a new tab, that means a beautiful page that works immediately. Make guidance optional and reversible. A “replay tour” button costs you nothing. Prefer defaults over questions. Every setting you ask about on day one is a reason to leave. Cut clever ideas that need explaining. Clear beats clever. What’s next Version 3.0 has just shipped on Chrome, Edge and Firefox, so it’s too early for solid numbers. I’ll watch day-one retention closely over the next few months and share what I learn in a follow-up post. If you want to see the new first-run experience for yourself, WanaGo is free: Chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/bgaeojjcodgaioepdilnejpegpehfgcg Microsoft Edge: https://microsoftedge.microsoft.com/addons/detail/kgidbfmjmkjcoilafhfdpgggjioiaamo Firefox: https://addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/wanago-new-tab/ Website: https://www.wanagonewtab.com And if you’ve built onboarding for an extension or app, I’d love to hear what worked for you in the comments.
